A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multi-reward multi-policy evaluation work and MR-NaS framework. The main text, equations, figures, algorithms, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations in four tabular environments, including learning curves, experiments across environment sizes, and a numerical sample-complexity analysis.

after.justification: v2 reports original tabular simulations in Section 6 and Appendix C, including revised learning curves and retained sample-complexity calculations.

M1.justification: MR-NaS retains the same relaxed-rate objective, certainty-equivalent allocation, forced exploration mixture, model updates, and stopping rule. The revised optimization derivations and additional solver documentation do not establish a different exploration algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Riverswim, Forked Riverswim, DoubleChain, and NArms under finite-reward multi-policy, reward-free multi-policy, and reward-free single-policy scenarios. Figure 5's Riverswim analysis with cube and norm-bounded reward sets is also retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same methods: SF-NR, GVFExplorer, and both noisy-policy variants for finite rewards; SF-NR and both noisy variants for reward-free multi-policy evaluation; and both noisy variants for reward-free single-policy evaluation. Newly cited methods are not added as experimental comparators.

E3.justification: v2 Appendix C.4 describes batched evaluation every F steps, but leaves F unspecified and retains Section 6's statement that evaluation occurs at each time-step. The new sampling details are not identified as changes to earlier experiments. Consequently, a change in the evaluation procedure cannot be reliably established.

E4.justification: The existing state-size sensitivity evidence in Figures 10–11 is revised. For example, at the largest NArms size in Figure 10, MR-NaS changes from finishing above several comparator error curves to below them. The size ranges and analytical questions remain the same, with no new ablation or robustness axis.

E5.justification: Both versions report 30 seeds and bootstrap-based 95% confidence intervals. Changed confidence-band widths do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figures 3 and 10 substantially revise finite-reward learning curves across the four environments and multiple sizes. In Figure 3's NArms panel, MR-NaS finishes above GVFExplorer and the noisy-policy curves in v1 but below them in v2. Some reward-free multi-policy curves also change in Figures 4 and 11. These are revised reported outcomes; the PDFs do not establish identical underlying settings for attributing cross-version performance gains.

T1.justification: Proposition 4.1 replaces an exact equivalence with separate necessary and sufficient bounds. Lemma B.2 changes its discount dependence from (1−γ)^2 to (1−γ)^4, and Proposition B.7 replaces recurrent-class indicators with hitting-probability vectors. The old Lemma B.8 is qualified and reproved as Lemma 4.4/B.8; Proposition B.9 and the relaxed-rate proof are substantially revised. v1's erroneous polytope optimization in Equation 14 is also replaced by a revised formulation in v2 Equation 16.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: an instance-dependent PAC lower bound, worst-policy–reward-pair complexity, a tractable relaxation including reward-free evaluation, and an MR-NaS adaptation with asymptotic guarantees and tabular evidence.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 corrects v1's interpretation that increasing accuracy tolerance or decreasing the discount factor may increase confusing models and sample complexity; v2 gives the opposite direction. It also qualifies the empty-alternative case as a minimal learning challenge, explains the 2ε separation, and acknowledges possible lower-bound looseness.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-repository link and documents target-policy generation, sampling without replacement, finite reward-set size, and fixed single-policy targets. Appendices B.2.5 and C.4 also add warm-started CVXPY solver information and value-computation details. These are additional disclosures rather than established changes to the experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Mukherjee et al. on tree-MDP evaluation, Weissmann et al. on bandit excess-risk guarantees, and Papini et al. on behavioral-policy optimization, alongside additional bandit and CVXPY citations. This broadens the contextual comparison while preserving the paper's central positioning relative to Best Policy Identification.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose remain intact, with targeted explanatory rewrites. Section 5 is renamed to 'MR-NaS for Policy Evaluation,' computational material is organized into Appendix B.2.5, Appendix C.4 gains experimental-detail subsections, and an Impact Statement is added.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main paper and references from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with running headers and extensive resizing and relocation of figures, algorithms, and theorem boxes. Several result plots change legend order and axis ranges. The numbered figure set and notation table are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial mathematical deficiencies in Proposition 4.1, Lemma B.2, Proposition B.7, and the relaxed-rate argument, and replaces v1's unbounded polytope formulation with a meaningful linear program. These repairs materially strengthen the theoretical foundation of the paper. Added computational and experimental documentation also helps reproducibility. Evaluation-frequency ambiguity and unexplained curve revisions remain limitations, so the improved assessment rests principally on the theoretical repairs rather than higher plotted performance.
